body.heading: A lever you turn
paragraphs: Bicycle gears do the same job as a lever: they trade distance for force. The chain connects a toothed ring at the pedals to a smaller or larger sprocket at the back wheel, and the sizes of the two decide how many times the wheel turns for each turn of the pedals.

In a high gear, one pedal turn spins the wheel several times — fast on flat ground, but each push must be hard. In a low gear the wheel turns barely once per pedal turn, so each push is easier but the bike advances less.

body.heading: Counting teeth
paragraphs: The ratio is simple arithmetic. If the front ring has 44 teeth and the rear sprocket 22, the wheel turns twice for every pedal turn. Swap to a rear sprocket with 34 teeth and the wheel turns only about 1.3 times — but your legs feel the hill shrink.

A derailleur makes the swap while moving: a spring-loaded arm pushes the chain sideways onto a neighbouring sprocket and takes up the slack. Modern bikes offer twenty or more combinations, though neighbouring gears overlap so much that the useful range is what matters, not the count.

body.heading: Why low gear wins hills
paragraphs: Climbing demands power against gravity, and your legs deliver power best at a comfortable pedalling rhythm. Low gears let you keep that rhythm — spinning easily at, say, 80 pedal turns a minute — while the bike crawls upward at walking pace.

It feels like cheating because the trade is invisible: you pedal more times to cover the same ground. The energy used is the same; the gears simply let you pay it in small, comfortable instalments instead of a few exhausting pushes.

description: Gears trade speed for force: a low gear turns the wheel less per pedal stroke, but with far more push.
